value.overview: The Black-breasted Wood-Quail is a secretive, ground-dwelling New World quail of humid mountain forests in Costa Rica and western Panama. It usually moves through dense understory in small family groups or coveys and is more often heard than seen. Its dark plumage, black breast, variable white throat, and barred lower breast help identify it. The species is closely associated with cool, wet forest conditions and spends most of its time walking among leaf litter and low vegetation.
value.classification: The Black-breasted Wood-Quail belongs to the family Odontophoridae, the New World quails, within the order Galliformes. Its scientific name is Odontophorus leucolaemus.
value.identification: This compact quail is about 23 cm long, with dark brown upperparts marked by fine black, rufous, and buff patterning. The face, neck, and much of the underparts are black, while the lower breast shows pale barring and the belly is warm brown. The throat varies considerably, from conspicuously white to nearly blackish with only limited pale markings. It has a dark bill, brown iris, and dull gray legs. Juveniles are generally browner and less sharply patterned.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama, although reliable modern records are concentrated in Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident of middle elevations, generally from about 700 to 1,850 m, in the Cordillera de Guanacaste and other northern ranges, the Cordillera de Tilarán, the Central Cordillera, and the Talamanca region. A separated population occurs around Dota. It favors cool, humid montane or cloud forest, dense understory, ravines, forest edges with cover, and mature secondary woodland.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and non-migratory in Costa Rica. Individuals remain within mountain forest territories throughout the year, although local movements may occur while groups forage or respond to changing food and cover conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but nesting in Costa Rica is associated with the beginning of the rainy season, especially May and June. The nest is a rounded hollow or chamber concealed in leaf litter, often on a sloping bank near a small ravine, with the entrance directed slightly downward. Clutches contain about four to six white eggs that may become stained brown. Incubation is reported to last approximately 16–17 days, and adults may cooperate in guarding the nest and young.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is not well documented. It probably consists mainly of seeds, fruits, berries, and other plant material collected from the forest floor, supplemented by insects and other small invertebrates. Groups forage by walking slowly through leaf litter and dense understory, probing and scratching for food. Feeding activity takes place during the day, often within a relatively small area used by the group.
value.behavior: Black-breasted Wood-Quails are shy, terrestrial, and strongly social. They commonly travel in coveys, often numbering several birds and sometimes around 10–15 individuals, while remaining concealed in thick vegetation. Groups defend territories through loud reciprocal calling, especially shortly after dawn. When approached, the birds usually walk or crouch away rather than fly, flushing only reluctantly. They may roost in low branches and maintain stable group associations across seasons.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend has not been reliably quantified. Local populations in Costa Rica may be affected by habitat fragmentation, but the species remains locally common in suitable mountain forest.
